# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

</document>

# Critical Reading: Varga and Holm, "Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem"

This comment does real work. Using the microdata, it uncovers facts the Halden paper misstated or left out, most importantly about attrition. It also replaces the pilot's two weakest inputs, the manager-reported output index and scheduled hours, with record-based output and actual hours. Most of its arithmetic checks out, and its data note is candid.

Its central conclusion is a different matter. The claim that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact" is not supported by its own corrected estimate. It is also contradicted by the randomised evidence the comment cites selectively.

## Arithmetic checks

| Item | Calculation | Reported | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Record vs manager gap | 98.9 − 95.1 | −3.8 | ✓ |
| Actual hours, 27 orgs | 34.6 / 40.3 = 0.859 | −14.1% | ✓ |
| Actual hours, 17 orgs | 34.8 / 40.4 = 0.861 | −13.9% | ✓ |
| Table 2, row 2 | 95.1 / 0.800 = 1.189 | +18.9% | ✓ |
| Table 2, row 3 | 98.4 / 0.859 = 1.146 | +14.6% | ✓ |
| Table 2, row 4 | 95.4 / 0.861 = 1.108 | +10.8% | ✓ |
| Real revenue | 1.014 / 1.041 = 0.974 | −2.6% | ✓ |
| **Hours decomposition** | 32 + (4 × 0.7) + 1.6 = **36.4** | 34.6 | **✗** |
| **Energy extrapolation** | 0.29 ÷ (0.32 / 3 months) ≈ 2.7 months after month 6 | "around month ten" | **≈ month 9** |

**The hours decomposition doesn't add up.** On a 32-hour schedule, 0.7 extra hours on each of four days plus 1.6 hours on the day off gives 36.4 hours, not 34.6. The reported 34.6 implies only about 0.25 extra hours a day. One of the figures is wrong:

- If 36.4 is right, actual hours fell by only about 10%, and the corrected per-hour gain would be smaller still.
- If 34.6 is right, the "+0.7 hours per day" description is wrong.

Either way, this needs fixing, because Table 2 depends on the hours figure.

The energy extrapolation is a minor slip. A straight line through the two survey points reaches zero at about month 9, not month 10.

## 1. Attrition is the strongest new finding, but it is not corrected

The Halden paper said the nine withdrawals happened "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons." According to the microdata, seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had started, and six cited workload or output. That is a material misstatement in the original paper. It turns a footnote into survivorship bias.

The comment overstates what it has done with this, though:

- **The abstract says** "correcting the first three" problems gives 10.8%. The first three problems listed are attrition, the output measure and hours. Table 2 corrects only output and hours. **Attrition is never corrected.** The 10.8% is still an estimate for survivors.
- **The size of the bias is never estimated.** Even a rough bound would help. For example, the comment could assume the nine withdrawers had zero per-hour gain, weight them by headcount, and show the effect. As it stands, the reader knows the direction of the bias but not its size.
- **The exit reasons account for only eight of the nine** organisations (six cited workload or output, two scheduling). This is minor, but it should be stated.

## 2. The record-based output measure has a problem of its own

The 3.8-point gap between manager and record measures, with managers higher in 19 of 23 cases, is good evidence of optimistic reporting. But one of the record types listed is **"billable hours delivered."** That is an input, not an output.

If billable hours count as output in some professional-services firms, then cutting hours lowers "output" almost automatically, whatever happens to productivity. Dividing that by hours to get output per hour is partly circular. This could push the record-based index *down* for those firms and so overstate the correction. The comment should show the comparison with billable-hours records excluded.

It is also fair to note that manager judgement can sometimes capture things that raw counts miss, such as complexity or quality. The gap is evidence of bias, but not proof that records are always the better measure.

## 3. The subsets are not random, and the direction of the selection is unknown

The data note says this honestly: the 17, 23 and 27 organisations used for corrections are self-selected by whether they kept records and time tracking. These are probably disproportionately software and professional-services firms, which had the highest manager-reported indices. The corrected estimates could therefore be biased in either direction relative to the full pilot.

The conclusion then generalises well beyond the subset. The data note says the estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole." The conclusion talks about "reduced-hours schemes" in general. Both cannot stand.

## 4. Revenue: the correction is right, but CPI is not quite the right deflator

The nominal-to-real correction is valid. I raised the same point about the original paper. But CPI measures consumer prices, not the prices these firms charge. Sector-specific or producer price deflators would be more appropriate.

The better benchmark would be revenue growth among comparable firms that did not take part, which the comment does not attempt. Its broader judgement, that revenue is a poor proxy for productivity, is correct.

## 5. Sectoral claims: largely right, but the evidence is thin and used selectively

The comment's point about the per-hour metric (any output index above 80 registers as a gain) matches my reading of the original. Its use of the evidence has problems, though:

- **The retail correction rests on three organisations.** The −11.2% figure is suggestive at most.
- **It compares two different measures.** Halden's retail figure is a change in an output index for each organisation over time. Varden's −11.4% is output per FTE relative to a control group, in counters where opening hours were kept the same. Halden retailers may have handled coverage differently. The two numbers agree, but that agreement may be partly coincidence.
- **It is selective about Varden.** It calls the Varden counter stratum "the most reliable finding in the literature" (10 offices, wide CI). But Varden's case-processing stratum was also randomised and registered, used record-based output and actual hours, and was larger. It found **+12.5% output per actual hour (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4)** against a control group at month 9. The comment does not mention this.

## 6. The novelty argument carries the whole conclusion and is not tested

After the corrections, a gain of about 11% remains. "Entirely an artifact" therefore depends completely on the novelty argument. That argument is speculative, and the comment had the data to test it but did not:

- **Energy is not output.** A decline in self-reported energy does not show that productivity declined.
- **Halden collected output monthly.** The comment has the microdata. If output per hour fell from month three to month six, as novelty predicts, that could be checked directly. It wasn't, or at least it wasn't reported.
- **A straight line through two data points is not a trend.** Energy could level off above baseline as easily as fall to zero.
- **Varden partly addresses novelty.** The case-processing gain held at month 9, and the control offices also knew they were being evaluated, which removes part of the "under evaluation" effect. Varden's 24-month follow-up will be more informative still.
- **The burden of proof applies in both directions.** It is fair to say that durability has not been shown. "Entirely an artifact" is itself a positive claim, and it needs evidence too.

The defensible conclusion is that durability is unknown. The comment's own recommendation of at least 18 months of follow-up implicitly accepts this.

## 7. The meetings critique misdescribes the Varden analysis

Varden presented the meetings analysis as exploratory. The authors said a seven-office correlation "cannot establish a mechanism," and they registered a confirmatory test. The comment's description differs from what Varden reported:

- **"A subgroup selected for analysis after the results were known."** The seven offices were all the treated case-processing offices, which was a stratum fixed before randomisation. The meeting data were collected in month six, before the nine-month results existed. The analysis was not pre-registered, but the subgroup was not cherry-picked after the fact.
- **"Should not be cited as a mechanism."** Varden never claimed it as an established mechanism. The comment is arguing against a stronger claim than the one Varden made.
- **The comment confuses "not caused by rest" with "artifact."** If cutting meetings explains the gain, then the gain is *real*. It would just come from removing low-value time rather than from rest. That would be a reason to doubt that the hours cut itself is necessary, not a reason to call the gain spurious.

Varden's own figures also offer support the comment doesn't engage with. Meetings fell by 3.3 hours, and actual hours fell by 4.9.

## How the three documents fit together

| Question | Halden pilot | Varden RCT | Varga and Holm |
|---|---|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, non-coverage work | +23.4% (scheduled hours, manager-rated) | +12.5% (actual hours, records, controlled) | +10.8% (survivors, subset, no control) |
| Coverage-bound work | Output −6.9%, "sector-general" | Output/FTE −11.4%, worse service | Agrees with Varden |
| Durability | Not tested | 9 months, 24-month follow-up under way | Asserted as novelty, not tested |
| Mechanism | Fatigue (asserted) | Meetings (exploratory) | Rejects meetings and rest; offers none |

The two independent estimates of the corrected gain, Varden's controlled +12.5% and Varga and Holm's uncontrolled +10.8%, are close. That is evidence *against* the "entirely an artifact" conclusion, not for it.

## Bottom line

**Well supported by this comment:**
- Halden misreported when and why organisations withdrew, and its sample is a sample of survivors.
- Manager-reported output overstated record-based output by about 4 points.
- Actual hours fell by about 14%, not 20%. The breakdown of where the hours went needs fixing.
- Halden's headline gain of 23.4% is roughly double what corrected measures support.
- Real revenue probably fell slightly.
- Reduced hours with unchanged coverage reduce output in presence-bound work.

**Not supported:**
- That the remaining gain is "entirely" an artifact. The comment's own estimate is about +11%, Varden's randomised estimate is +12.5%, and novelty is asserted rather than tested.
- That the meetings finding came from a post hoc subgroup.
- Any generalisation from the corrected subsets to reduced-hours schemes as a whole, which the comment's own data note rules out.

**What would settle the open questions:**
- The month-by-month output trend in the Halden microdata.
- An attrition-bounded estimate.
- Record-based output with billable-hours measures excluded.
- Varden's 24-month results, including the confirmatory test of the meetings mechanism.
